explanation: A resource (memory, a file handle, a lock, a socket) is bound to an object's lifetime: acquisition happens in the constructor, release happens in the destructor. Because C++ guarantees destructors run when a scope exits — including via an exception — RAII makes cleanup automatic and exception-safe without try/finally.
why: In HFT code, RAII is how you keep hot paths exception-safe without manual cleanup logic — lock_guard, unique_ptr, and scoped socket wrappers are all RAII.

explanation: Every C++ expression has a value category. An lvalue names an object with identity you can take the address of (a variable). A prvalue (pure rvalue) is a temporary that initializes an object (like `42` or a function return by value). An xvalue ("eXpiring value") denotes an object near the end of its lifetime whose resources can be reused — the result of std::move or a function returning T&&. glvalue = lvalue or xvalue (has identity); rvalue = prvalue or xvalue (can be moved from).
code:
int x = 10;      // x is an lvalue
int y = x + 1;    // (x + 1) is a prvalue
int&& r = std::move(x); // std::move(x) is an xvalue
why: Overload resolution between T&, const T&, and T&& — and therefore whether a copy or a move constructor runs — is decided entirely by the value category of the argument expression.

explanation: Move construction/assignment transfers ownership of a resource (a heap buffer, a file descriptor) from a source object to a destination instead of deep-copying it, leaving the source in a valid-but-unspecified state. It's enabled by rvalue-reference (T&&) overloads that the compiler prefers when the argument is an rvalue.
why: Avoiding needless deep copies of order-book snapshots, strings, and vectors on hot paths is one of the single biggest, cheapest latency wins in C++ — this is why interviewers probe it so heavily.

explanation: std::move unconditionally casts its argument to an rvalue reference (T&&) — it doesn't move anything itself, it just enables a move overload to be selected. std::forward conditionally casts: inside a template taking a forwarding reference (T&&), it forwards the argument as an lvalue if it was passed as one, and as an rvalue if it was passed as one — preserving the caller's value category ("perfect forwarding").
why: Wrapper/factory functions (make_unique-style, emplace_back) rely on this to avoid an extra copy when constructing objects in place.

explanation: A parameter declared as `T&&` where T is a deduced template parameter (not a fixed type) is a forwarding reference, not necessarily an rvalue reference — it binds to both lvalues and rvalues, with T deduced as `U&` for an lvalue argument and `U` for an rvalue argument. `Widget&&` for a concrete, non-template type Widget is always a plain rvalue reference, not a forwarding reference.
code:
template <class T> void f(T&& x);  // forwarding reference: T deduced
void g(Widget&& x);                // NOT forwarding: Widget is fixed, plain rvalue ref
why: Misreading a forwarding reference as "just an rvalue reference" is a classic interview trap and a real source of bugs in generic low-latency container code.

explanation: Return Value Optimization lets the compiler construct a returned object directly in the caller's storage, skipping a copy/move entirely. Since C++17, elision for a prvalue returned directly (`return T(...);` or `return make(...)`) is mandatory by the standard. Named RVO (returning a named local variable) is still only an optional-but-near-universal optimization, not guaranteed.
why: Explains why returning large objects by value is often free in modern C++ — no need to reach for output parameters "for performance" the way you might in older C++.

explanation: Rule of Three (pre-C++11): if a class needs a custom destructor, copy constructor, or copy-assignment operator, it almost certainly needs all three (it's managing a resource). Rule of Five extends this to include move constructor and move-assignment for efficient resource transfer. Rule of Zero: prefer designing classes that own no raw resources directly (use existing RAII types like std::vector/std::unique_ptr as members) so the compiler-generated special members are already correct — no manual rule-of-five code needed.
why: Rule of Zero is the modern default; Rule of Five is what you write only when your class IS the resource-owning primitive (like implementing your own smart pointer).

explanation: A class with virtual functions gets a hidden vtable (a static array of function pointers, one per virtual function) and each instance carries a vptr pointing to its class's vtable. A virtual call is an indirect call through this pointer, resolved at runtime based on the object's dynamic type — enabling polymorphism, at the cost of an extra pointer dereference and the loss of inlining/branch prediction the compiler could otherwise apply to a direct call.
why: Virtual dispatch is a real, measurable cost on a hot path (indirection + inlining barrier) — this is why HFT codebases often use CRTP/templates instead of virtual functions where the call is in a tight loop.

explanation: A pure virtual function (`virtual ret f(...) = 0;`) has no implementation in that class and makes the class abstract — it cannot be instantiated directly, only through a derived class that overrides every pure virtual function. It's how C++ expresses an interface.

If a class will ever be deleted through a base-class pointer, its destructor must be virtual. Otherwise `delete basePtr;` only calls the base destructor, skipping the derived class's cleanup — undefined behavior, and in practice a resource/memory leak.
why: A very common "what's wrong with this code" interview snippet — omit `virtual` on the base destructor and ask what leaks.

explanation: When a class inherits from two classes that both inherit from a common base, the derived class ends up with two separate copies of the common base's members by default, causing ambiguity. Declaring the intermediate inheritance as `virtual` (virtual inheritance) makes both paths share a single common base subobject instead.

Marking parameters, member functions, and variables `const` wherever they aren't meant to be mutated lets the compiler catch accidental mutation at compile time and documents intent. A `const` member function promises not to modify the object's observable state (mutable members aside) and can be called on const objects/references.

`const` means "this value won't change after initialization" but the value may still only be known at runtime. `constexpr` means "this must be computable at compile time" (given constexpr-compatible inputs), enabling compile-time evaluation, use in template arguments/array bounds, and often literally baking the result into the binary.
code:
const int a = someRuntimeFunction();   // fine: const, but not compile-time
constexpr int b = 2 * 21;              // must be evaluable at compile time
int arr[b];                             // OK, b is a compile-time constant
// int arr2[a];                        // error if a isn't compile-time constant

explanation: Static (compile-time) binding resolves which function is called based on the static type of the expression — this is how non-virtual functions and overload resolution work. Dynamic (runtime) binding resolves the call based on the object's actual runtime type via the vtable — this is how virtual function calls work when invoked through a base pointer/reference.

Three standard levels: (1) basic guarantee — if an exception is thrown, no resources leak and invariants hold, but the object's exact state is unspecified; (2) strong guarantee — the operation either fully succeeds or has no visible effect at all (commit-or-rollback), often implemented via copy-and-swap; (3) nothrow/no-throw guarantee — the operation is guaranteed never to throw, which is required for things like destructors, swap, and move operations to be safely usable by the standard library.
why: Move constructors should be `noexcept` whenever possible — std::vector will only use the move constructor during reallocation if it's marked noexcept, otherwise it silently falls back to copying for exception safety.

explanation: A class Derived inherits from a template Base<Derived>, letting Base call methods on the derived type at compile time (via static_cast<Derived*>(this)) instead of through a virtual function. This gives compile-time ("static") polymorphism — no vtable, no indirect call, full inlining — at the cost of losing runtime polymorphism (you can't hold a heterogeneous collection of Base<T>* and call through it uniformly).
why: CRTP is exactly how a lot of low-latency C++ gets polymorphism-like code reuse without paying the virtual-call cost on the hot path.

explanation: A template is a blueprint; the compiler generates ("instantiates") a concrete function/class for each distinct set of template arguments actually used, at compile time. This gives zero-overhead generic code (no runtime type dispatch) but increases compile time and binary size ("code bloat") if many instantiations are generated.
code:
template <class T>
T max_of(T a, T b) { return a > b ? a : b; }
max_of(3, 5);      // instantiates max_of<int>
max_of(3.0, 5.0);  // instantiates a SEPARATE max_of<double>

term: SFINAE (Substitution Failure Is Not An Error)
explanation: When the compiler substitutes template arguments into a candidate function's signature during overload resolution, a substitution that would produce an ill-formed type/expression is silently removed from the candidate set instead of being a hard compile error — as long as the ill-formed part is in the immediate context (like the return type or a parameter type), not inside the function body.
why: Modern code increasingly replaces hand-rolled SFINAE with C++20 concepts/requires-clauses for the same effect with much clearer compiler errors — interviewers may ask you to explain both and why concepts are preferred now.

explanation: Concepts let you name and enforce a compile-time constraint on template parameters directly (e.g. "T must be arithmetic"), replacing much of what SFINAE was previously used for, with far more readable code and much clearer compiler errors when a constraint isn't satisfied.

A class hides its private implementation details behind a pointer to a forward-declared, fully-defined-only-in-the-.cpp implementation struct. Changing private members no longer changes the public class's size or triggers a full recompile of every translation unit that includes its header — trading one extra heap allocation and indirection for much better compile-time isolation and ABI stability.

When calling an unqualified function, the compiler also looks in the namespaces associated with the function call's argument types (not just the local/enclosing/global scope). This is why `std::swap(a, b)` for user types often just works as `swap(a, b)` unqualified — ADL finds a `swap` defined in the argument's own namespace.

Every non-inline function, object, class, and template specialization must have exactly one definition across the whole program (inline entities may be defined identically in multiple translation units). Violating it — e.g. defining a non-inline function differently in two .cpp files that both get linked — is typically undefined behavior, often only caught at link time (duplicate-symbol errors) or silently producing inconsistent behavior.

In modern C++, `inline` primarily changes linkage, not compiler inlining behavior: it permits a function or variable to be defined identically in multiple translation units without violating ODR (the linker merges them), which is why header-defined functions must be marked inline. The compiler decides whether to actually inline a call independently, based on its own cost heuristics (or `__attribute__((always_inline))`/`[[gnu::always_inline]]` if you need to force it).
code:
// header.h — safe to include in many .cpp files because of `inline`
inline int square(int x) { return x * x; }

term: Undefined Behavior vs Unspecified vs Implementation-defined
explanation: Undefined behavior (UB) means the standard imposes no requirements at all — anything can happen, including things that look like they "work" (signed integer overflow, dereferencing a dangling pointer, data races). Unspecified behavior means the standard allows multiple valid outcomes without requiring the implementation to document which one it picked (e.g. argument evaluation order pre-C++17). Implementation-defined behavior is unspecified behavior that each implementation MUST document (e.g. the size of `int`).
code:
int x = INT_MAX;
x = x + 1;              // signed overflow: UB, not just "wraps around"
f(g(), h());             // pre-C++17: unspecified which of g()/h() evaluates first
std::cout << sizeof(int); // implementation-defined, but documented by each compiler
why: Interviewers love asking "what does this print" for code whose real answer is "it's UB, so this is the wrong question" — recognizing UB is often the point of the question.

explanation: Every type has an alignment requirement (an address must be a multiple of it), and the compiler inserts padding bytes between struct members so each satisfies its alignment — meaning struct size and field order matter, and reordering members from largest-to-smallest alignment usually shrinks a struct.
why: In HFT, packing order-book/message structs tightly (and aligning them to cache-line boundaries where you WANT padding, e.g. to avoid false sharing) is a routine performance exercise.

explanation: When two variables used by different threads happen to sit on the same CPU cache line, writes by one thread invalidate the other thread's cached copy even though they touch logically unrelated data — causing expensive cache-coherence traffic that looks like contention but isn't. The fix is padding/aligning hot per-thread variables to separate cache lines, typically 64 bytes, using `alignas(64)`.
why: One of the single most common real HFT interview questions: "two threads write to adjacent memory — what happens, and how do you fix it?"

explanation: The C++11 memory model defines, for multithreaded programs, which writes by one thread are guaranteed visible to reads by another thread. Without synchronization (atomics, mutexes), concurrent unsynchronized access to the same memory from multiple threads where at least one is a write is a data race — undefined behavior, not just "a wrong value." Synchronization establishes a happens-before relationship that makes prior writes visible.

std::atomic<T> operations are indivisible and can specify an ordering constraint. `memory_order_relaxed` only guarantees atomicity, no ordering with other memory operations. `memory_order_acquire` (on a load) prevents subsequent reads/writes from being reordered before it; `memory_order_release` (on a store) prevents preceding reads/writes from being reordered after it — together they form the classic "release a flag, acquire a flag" handoff pattern. `memory_order_seq_cst` (the default) additionally gives a single total order across all seq_cst operations, at higher synchronization cost.
code:
std::atomic<int> counter{0};
counter.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed); // just needs atomicity, not ordering
why: Relaxed atomics are how HFT code gets lock-free counters/sequence numbers without paying for a full memory fence when no ordering guarantee is actually needed.

explanation: A lambda's capture clause controls how it accesses enclosing-scope variables: `[x]` captures x by value (a copy taken at lambda creation), `[&x]` by reference (must outlive the lambda — a classic dangling-reference bug if the lambda escapes its scope), `[=]`/`[&]` capture everything used by value/reference respectively, and `[x = std::move(y)]` (C++14 generalized/init captures) lets you move or compute the captured value.

Assigning or passing a derived-class object to a base-class object BY VALUE truncates ("slices") it — only the base subobject is copied, and any derived-specific data/virtual overrides are lost, because the target's static type is Base, not Derived.
why: Fix: take the parameter by reference or pointer (`Base&`/`Base*`) instead of by value, so no copy/slicing happens and virtual dispatch still works.

term: Function overloading vs overriding vs hiding
explanation: Overloading: multiple functions with the same name but different parameter lists in the same scope, resolved at compile time. Overriding: a derived class redefines a VIRTUAL function with an identical signature, resolved at runtime. Hiding: a derived class declares a function with the SAME NAME as a base function (any signature) that is NOT an override — this hides ALL base overloads of that name from ordinary unqualified lookup on the derived type, a frequent source of surprise bugs.

Container-modifying operations can invalidate existing iterators/references/pointers into that container, and the exact rule differs per container: `std::vector` invalidates ALL iterators on reallocation (and end() on any insert/erase), `std::deque` invalidates on insert/erase almost anywhere except sometimes at the ends, `std::list`/`std::map`/`std::set`/`std::unordered_map` only invalidate iterators to the specific erased element — others remain valid. Using an invalidated iterator is undefined behavior.
why: A frequent "what's wrong with this loop" style debugging question, e.g. erasing from a vector while iterating with a for-range loop.

explanation: `std::unique_ptr<T>` expresses sole ownership — move-only, zero overhead over a raw pointer, deletes the object when it goes out of scope. `std::shared_ptr<T>` expresses shared ownership via atomic reference counting — the object is destroyed when the last shared_ptr referencing it is destroyed; copying it is not free (atomic increment/decrement). `std::weak_ptr<T>` observes a shared_ptr-managed object without extending its lifetime or affecting the ref count, used to break reference cycles and to safely check "is this object still alive?".
code:
auto owner = std::make_unique<Widget>();      // sole owner
auto shared = std::make_shared<Widget>();       // ref-counted
std::weak_ptr<Widget> observer = shared;        // doesn't keep it alive
if (auto locked = observer.lock()) { /* still alive */ }
why: On a latency-sensitive path, prefer unique_ptr (or raw pointers/references with clear ownership) over shared_ptr — the atomic refcount traffic is a real, measurable cost.

explanation: STL containers take an Allocator template parameter controlling how they obtain raw memory (default: `operator new`/`operator delete`), which is how you plug in an arena/pool/stack allocator to avoid general-purpose heap allocation on a hot path — heap allocation involves locking, bookkeeping, and unpredictable latency, all of which HFT code tries to avoid at runtime.

Most std::string implementations avoid a heap allocation for short strings (commonly up to 15-22 bytes depending on the standard library) by storing the character data directly inline inside the string object's own storage instead of on the heap — only longer strings actually heap-allocate a buffer.
code:
std::string s = "short";     // typically stored inline, no heap allocation
std::string big(100, 'x');   // too long for SSO -> heap-allocates
why: Explains why short-string operations in a hot loop are often much cheaper than intuition ("strings always heap allocate") suggests — though it's still worth avoiding std::string entirely on the hottest paths in favor of fixed buffers or string_view.

explanation: A non-owning, lightweight view (pointer + length) over a contiguous sequence of characters — no allocation, no copy, no ownership. It's ideal for read-only string parameters, but the viewed data must outlive the string_view, and a string_view is not guaranteed to be null-terminated.
Lets you unpack a tuple/pair/struct/array into named variables in one declaration, improving readability over `.first`/`.second` or `std::get<N>`.

`std::optional<T>` represents a value that may or may not be present, without resorting to a sentinel value or a pointer. `std::variant<A,B,...>` is a type-safe tagged union holding exactly one of a fixed set of alternative types, checked/visited safely instead of via a raw union + manual tag. `std::any` holds a value of any copyable type, type-erased, retrieved via `any_cast` — the most flexible but also the least type-safe/least performant of the three.

Declaring a function `noexcept` promises it will never let an exception propagate out (if one does anyway, `std::terminate` is called immediately — it is NOT converted into a caught exception). Beyond documentation, it matters functionally: standard containers like std::vector only use a type's move constructor during reallocation if that move constructor is noexcept; otherwise they conservatively fall back to copying to preserve the strong exception-safety guarantee.

The relative initialization order of non-local static/global objects DEFINED IN DIFFERENT TRANSLATION UNITS is unspecified by the standard. If one such global's constructor depends on another already being initialized, the program may crash or misbehave depending on link order — this is the "static initialization order fiasco." The common fix is the "construct on first use" idiom: wrap the global in a function returning a reference to a function-local static, which C++11 guarantees is initialized exactly once, on first call, in a thread-safe way.
